study.title: A counterexample to the quantum Hedetniemi conjecture

cover.headline: A conjecture about quantum graph coloring **lasted 12 years until this counterexample arrived.**

slides.title: When you multiply two graphs, the quantum coloring difficulty should match the easier factor.
slides.body:
In quantum graph theory, researchers assumed that if you take the categorical product of two graphs, the quantum chromatic number of the product would equal whichever factor has the smaller quantum chromatic number. This seemed intuitive: the product shouldn't be harder to color than both parts.

The Hedetniemi conjecture for quantum chromatic numbers, posed by Godsil, Roberson, Šámal and Severini, predicted exactly this behavior. No counterexample had been found.

slides.title: The team reports constructing two graphs whose product is easier to color than either piece alone.
slides.body:
The researchers built explicit finite graphs G and H where the product has a classical chromatic number of at most 1538, while both factors have quantum chromatic numbers of at least 1539. The product is strictly easier to color than either factor.

They adapted Zhu's counterexample to the classical Hedetniemi conjecture by choosing a base graph where the Lovász theta number of the complement is large, and extended the argument to projection operators in noncommutative C*-algebras.

slides.title: The counterexample holds for spatial, approximate, commuting-operator and C*-algebraic variants of quantum coloring.
slides.body:
The team reports that their construction works for colorings by projections in any nonzero unital C*-algebra, covering every major variant of the quantum chromatic number. The result applies broadly across different mathematical formulations.

They also provide smaller counterexamples certified by exact integer data, and the entire construction has been formalized in Lean 4, a proof assistant that verifies mathematical arguments computationally.

caveats: This is a preprint posted to arXiv, not a peer-reviewed publication, so no independent expert has checked the constructions or proofs yet.
The result is purely about mathematical structures called graphs and their quantum chromatic numbers, not about physical quantum systems or practical coloring problems.

caption: A 12-year-old conjecture about quantum graph coloring just met its match. Researchers report constructing two graphs whose categorical product has a classical chromatic number of 1538, while both factors have quantum chromatic numbers of at least 1539. The construction adapts Zhu's counterexample to classical Hedetniemi by using a base graph where the Lovász theta number of the complement is large, then extends the argument to non-commuting projection operators. The entire proof, including graph constructions and certificates, has been formalized in Lean 4. This is a preprint on arXiv. The main limitation: no peer review yet. Full study: http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20690v1 — Send this to anyone who thinks quantum versions of hard problems always behave like their classical cousins.
